name: Parietal operculum cortex
summary: The parietal operculum is the part of the parietal lobe that folds under the posterior lateral sulcus above the posterior insula and the planum temporale, behind the central operculum. It contains the secondary somatosensory cortex (SII) and the parieto-insular vestibular cortex, so it is the cortex of tactile object recognition, of the affective dimension of pain, and of the conscious sense of head motion and verticality. It is a middle cerebral artery territory, and its lesions produce impaired stereognosis and tactile learning, altered pain perception, and vertigo or tilt illusions; seizures here give bilateral tingling, pain or a sense of motion.

anatomy.location: Buried parietal cortex forming the roof of the posterior Sylvian fissure between the central operculum in front and the supramarginal gyrus behind, above the planum temporale and the posterior insula.

afferents.via: short association fibers and corpus callosum

afferents.from: Ventral posterior thalamus and posterior nuclear group

function: SII receives touch and proprioception from both sides of the body through the primary somatosensory cortex and the thalamus, with the two hands represented together, and it integrates them for recognizing objects by touch, learning tactile skills and attending to a stimulus; it also receives nociceptive input and, with the insula and cingulate, gives pain its unpleasant and motivational quality. The adjacent parieto-insular vestibular cortex combines vestibular, visual and neck proprioceptive signals to perceive self-motion and the vertical. Both sides of the body are represented, so a unilateral lesion produces subtler and bilateral tactile deficits than a postcentral lesion.

bestView.label: parietal operculum above the posterior insula
roof of the posterior Sylvian fissure

imaging.normalAppearance: The upper bank of the posterior Sylvian fissure on coronal images through the posterior insula, between the postcentral gyrus above and the planum temporale below.

pathology.finding: Small cortical restricted diffusion at the parietal operculum with impaired stereognosis, tactile extinction and sometimes vertigo.
Bilateral or contralateral tingling, painful auras or a sensation of rotation; scalp EEG shows a centro-parietal focus.
Lesion involving the parietal operculum, insula or thalamus with delayed burning pain and allodynia in the contralateral limbs.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the SII integration of touch and proprioception

lesionEffects.deficit: Altered pain perception or central pain
lesionEffects.mechanism: Damage to the opercular-insular nociceptive cortex

lesionEffects.deficit: Vertigo, tilt and loss of the subjective vertical
lesionEffects.mechanism: Involvement of the parieto-insular vestibular cortex

examination: Stereognosis: identify coins and keys placed in the hand with eyes closed
Bilateral simultaneous tactile stimulation for extinction
Subjective visual vertical (ask the patient to set a line upright) and a history of tilt illusions
pearls: SII is bilateral: a unilateral lesion impairs tactile recognition subtly, not with anesthesia
Painful seizures are rare and almost always parietal opercular or insular
The vestibular cortex sits here: cortical vertigo exists and is not a brainstem sign

pitfalls: Astereognosis with intact primary sensation is cortical; do not attribute it to a neuropathy
